1. Wing (f), wall N. Red plinth with panels with carpet edges: yellow middle area: side panels with architectural glimpses on the sides of a central compartment (?). IV style.

2. Wing (f), N wall, section E. Detail of the red plinth, in which the stylized aedicule structure is formed by a border of carpet that simulates a turned ribbon. Another simpler border, with a single line, completes the decoration. IV style.

4. Peristyle (g), wall E. Black plinth. Middle area: red panels with squares separated by narrow black compartments with candelabras. III style. The brick columns that supported the portico are visible.
3. Wing(f), E wall, N. Red plinth and yellow middle area. IV style.
5. Peristyle (g), wallE. Front view, cf. above, fig. 4. 77 N34388
7. Peristyle (g), wall E, central section. See Fig. 6. 77 N34384

6. Peristyle (g), wall E, section N. Detail of the black plinth and the middle area with red panels separated by a narrow black compartment containing a golden twisted candelabrum. III style. 77 N34386
8. Peristyle (g), wall E, section S. See above, fig. 6. 77 N34382
9. Peristyle (g), wall E, S. section Black plinth and middle area with black compartment and red panel with painting. III style.
10. Peristyle (g), wall E, section S. Detail of fig. 8: the base of the twisted candelabrum depicted in the middle area. III style. 77 N34387
11. Peristyle (g), wall E, section S. Detail of figure 9: picture with still life with tragic masks relating to the myth of Perseus and Andromeda (18 x 32). III style.

13. The medallion with the portrait of a child crowned with a vine reproduced in this nineteenth-century drawing (E. Eichler 1875, DAIR archive) was inserted within one of the panels of the room (h) or the triclinium (m).
12. Room (h), wall E, section N. Moulded stucco frame.
14. Triclinium (m), NE corner. Black plinth, middle area with red panels, black frieze. III style.
15. Triclinium (m), SE angle. Black Hoof; middle area: red side panel divided by a candelabrum that supported a medallion with bust; black frieze and white upper area. III style.
17. Triclinium (m), W wall, N. Black plinth section and red middle area. III style.
16. Triclinium (m), S wall, section E. Detail of the previous figure. The medallion with portrait that adorned the side panel can be glimpsed. III style.

1. Back room (b), wall N. Plinth and middle area white: panels and compartments squared by red lines. 77 N34391
2. Back room (b), wall N. See the previous figure. The decoration followed the course of the staircase leading to the upper floor. 77 N34390

2. Atrium(a), S. Zoccolo red wall with plants; Middle area: red panels separated by narrow yellow compartments. The panels contained still lifes in the center (birds and fruit, competitive vases). IV style. On the left you can see a painted niche (see fig. 3).
1. Atrium (a), wall E, section S. Red plinth with plants. IV style.

3. Atrium (a), S. The ceiling of the niche painted in white, yellow and red bands in a phase prior to that preserved on the walls of the room, and subsequently tapped to make the new plaster adhere better.  TT N34397

4. Wing (c), wall E. The decoration consists of a red plinth with simple geometric parting, a middle area with a red central panel and yellow side panels and a simple moulded stucco frame; it could still be dated to the phase of the III style.
5. Wing(c), angle S-E. Red plinth and midway with yellow side panels. Beyond the molded stucco frame, the painting continues in the upper area. III style (?).

6. Tablinum (d), wall N. The painting of this room can certainly be dated to the fourth style, as can be seen from the typical decoration of the red plinth, which alternates the compartments with large panels with plants. Only a few traces of the white middle area are preserved. 77 N34395
7. Tablinum (d), N wall, section O. Detail of the red plinth, with panel and compartment with plants. IV style. 77 N34396
8. Tablinum (d), wall E. See above, fig. 7.

9. National Museum of Naples. Opus sectile picture with slate background and palombino inlays, antique yellow and serpentine, depicting Venus tying her sandal, from the N wall of the triclinium (f). Third quarter of the first century A.D.
11. Triclinium (f), N wall, section O with recessed bed. Red hoof. III style (?).
10. Triclinium (f), wall N central section: the imprint left by the painting in the previous figure.
12. Triclinium (f), S. Wall Stucco frame with ovoli and arrows. III style (?).

13. Triclinium (f), W wall. It is the wall that preserves the greatest remains of the decoration: the artition of the plinth can no longer be distinguished. The middle area has, in the central red panel, the remains of a painting (43 cm wide), probably already destroyed at the time of the excavation; The middle panel is separated from the yellow side panels by means of narrow green compartments. Molded stucco frame. III style (?). 77 N34403

14. Triclinium (f), W wall, central section. Detail of the molded stucco frame, above which there must have been another, which concluded the lunette also decorated in stucco relief. The rectangular window overlooks the Via di Stabiae.
15. Viridarium (i), wall E, section N. Garden painting. IV style.
16. Viridarium (i), wall E, section N. See fig. 15.
17. Viridarium (i), wall E, section N. See fig. 15. The gaps visible in the fresco are due to the different deterioration of the various colors.

1. Room (e), S wall, section E. Yellow plinth, plain and middle area with yellow orthostat. I style.

6. Oecus(f), walls NeE: plinth and middle area restored with cocciopesto plaster, painted with black panels according to Mau [Mau W, p. 62: III style ("wohl dritten Stils")].
7. Oecus (f), N wall: upper area with frieze, dentilled cornice, three rows of yellow and purple ashlars with yellow border. 77 N34433

8. Oecus(f), wall E, section S and wall S, section E: plinth and middle area restored with cocciopesto plaster; upper area with frieze, dentilled cornice, two rows of yellow and purple ashlars in relief stucco of the first style.

10. Cubicle (g), wall N, section O: remains of the first style decoration of the antechamber with three rows of ashlars arranged at the top, yellow, purple and red with a green border, surmounted by a white plan, a dentilled frame and a drip of white stucco.

9. Cubicle (g), N and E walls with first style decoration. The subdivision of the room into antechamber and alcove was highlighted, as usual in this period, not only by the different design of the wall decoration, but also by the floor decoration, which has been lost here.

11. Cubicle (g), wall E, alcove: decoration with imitation marble cladding or polychrome imitation masonry, now discoloured in the lower part (the colours indicated in brackets are those recorded by Mau W, p. 63): plinth (green); top (brightly colored mottled marble); middle area with purple and green orthostats; moulded frame of white stucco; upper area of two rows of yellow, red and imitation marble ashlars, arranged at the head and cut. 77 N34434

12. The mouth of the terracotta cistern (height 61 cm, diameter 4l cm) now deposited in the cubicle (g), was in the garden of the peristyle; The edge is worn by the passage of the rope. It does not belong to the oldest or even the most recent specimens of this class of material of the partridge type (Partridge 6, p. 34).

13. Terracotta statue of a seated sorrowful old man (height 60 cm), whose left hand grasps the wrist of the right holding a scroll: it is a Greek scientist or philosopher, identified now with the physician Herophilus who studied the system of veins, now with Antisthenes or with Epicurus (for the beard), now with a tragic poet.
1. Atrium (b), view towards S. 81 FU 25607

2. Atrium (b), view towards the N, with impluvium and pedestal (of a marble statuette of Hercules) covered with polychrome marble. The lararium niche in the E wall of the vestibule (a) is visible, covered with marble with three holes in the shelf "one deeper than the others, probably intended to place small idols".

3. Atrium (b): table located to the S of the impluvium, composed of a single podium fluted with travertine and a shelf adorned with two lion heads of a finer travertine, if not of marble (Pernice T, pp. 7, 10, no. 18, fig. 5). The table must date back to the second century B.C. C. that is, the construction phase of the house. A confirmation of the high dating is provided by Varro (De lingua latina V, 125) who says that this type of table on a single support (columella) was fashionable at the time of his childhood.   81 FU25605
5. Cubicle (d), wall O, section S: recessed for the bed, frescoed in the fourth style with a white background with simple carpet edges.
4. Cubicle (d), S wall with splayed window, O wall with built-in bed.

6. Tablinum (e), wall O: drawing by G. Discanno in the DAIR archive (another drawing by Discanno, on a scale of 1:25, is preserved in Naples: ADS 5) of the landscape with Selene on the chariot pulled by winged horses and Endymion asleep in the lap of Hypnos (the personification of Sleep, with a white beard and wings) under a tree
7. Oecus(g), wall Oe wall N, section W: the red plinth with the meander adorned with rosettes is what remains of the frescoes, the middle area of which included a painting with Hercules.
8. Peristyle (m), E wall and niche covered with colored marble: note the capitals, now disappeared, documented by this photo from the '30s. DAIR 86331
9. Peristyle (m): niche leaning against wall E, covered with colored marble; the apse is painted with a curtain taken up on both sides.

10. Peristyle (m), niche leaning against wall E: detail of the basin of the apse frescoed with an umbrella canopy or a shell adorned with garlands and shoots that follow the course of the ribs, accentuating their curvature.  77 N34442

11. Statue in Parian marble of the early Hellenistic period depicting the Venus type Lovatelli, leaning on an archaizing idol, the so-called "Statue of the Virgin". Spes, found (with considerable remains of colour) in the niche of the E wall of the peristyle (m).
1. View of the N façade with the entrance to the caupona, the serving counter and the internal wall E with a niche (of lararium?) and holes for the beams of two shelves. 81 FU25590
1. Viridarium (f), wall N: lararium painting depicting Fortuna, globe with crescent and star and Bacchus, under garlands. Fiorelli D, p. 46
2. Atrium (a), N wall: the door of the triclinium (b) and the lararium niche (Boyce, no. 14).
1. Atrium (a), O wall, N section and N wall in opus incertum with the door of the triclinium (b) and lararium niche.

3. Triclinium (b), N wall with two overlapping decorations: the older one, painted on a white background, was tapped for the adhesion of the second layer consisting of a high protruding plinth of cocciopesto and an upper area of rough plaster.

4. Triclinium (b), S wall with two overlapping decorations: the older one, with a white background frescoed in the fourth style with a cupid in flight, was tapped for the adhesion of the second layer of cocciopesto plaster.
1. Façade of the workshop in opus listatum with rectangular holes, lined with bricks, of the beams of the hanging balcony that enlarged the pergula, the shopkeeper's home. Warsher 41
1. Façade with entrance 24 without the architrave. 81 FU25586
2. Façade in situ with limestone frame with entrance 24 and two slit windows typical of the second century B.C. C., subsequently walled up.

3. The entrance to the workshop at no. 25, made in the façade in the last period; jamb O is built in opus listatum, composed of a row of bricks and two rows of parallelepiped limestone blocks (and not a single row, as in most cases). Entrance 24, complete with the architrave, preserves the limestone frame construction dating back to the construction phase of the house in the second century BC.

4. Atrium (a), S wall with door and lararium niche. Under the niche appears the snake (now disappeared); on the sides of the niche were painted two wolves (So, ff. 16-18; "the one on the left lacks the head and neck; the one on the right is a wolf in the act of fleeing to the left; from its back comes out horizontally the bust of a virile figure with his arms stretched back".
5. VedutadaE: peristyle (c), summer triclinium and staircase; atrium (b) with two columns.
6. Peristyle (c), summer triclinium with masonry table. On the E side of the former peristyle we see three columns (in a very irregular opus listatum) incorporated into the opus incertum wall.

9. Tablinum (k), wall E: faded remains of the fresco in the third style: black plinth with geometric division "in crosses"; middle area (green?: Mau 1873A, p. 454) with central aedicule and frieze, discolored like the upper area.
7. Atrium (a), S wall: the arch of the lararium niche (Boyce, no. 16), with crescent moon. 77 N34446
8. Tablinum (k), N wall, central section, rest of the fresco in III style: black plinth with plants and ibises.  77 N34450

1. Façade with the vestibule of entrance 28, frescoed in the fourth style. On the brick jamb on the left, of the caupona at no. 29, the painted electoral inscription (now disappeared) L-C-S-II VIR (CIL IV 3380) was visible, which probably referred to the inhabitant of the nearby stately house I, 6, 15. The electoral inscription legible to the right of the entrance to the caupona referred instead to a member of the family living in the nearby House of the Citarist (I 4, 5.25): POPIDIVM AED ROG POLYBIVS (CIL IV 3379). On the front of the caupona serving counter appears the gap in the painted plaster, which contained the mosaic emblem depicting a theatrical mask.

2. Atrium (a): the four tuff columns with a base of two bulls and with Ionic capitals supported the valley barred by a railing. The W wall of the atrium, frescoed in the fourth style, is visible. DAIR 731235
4. Cubicle (e), N wall and E wall, N section: remains of the simple IV style decoration with a white background, with plinth and middle area with two panels separated by a narrow central compartment.

3. Cubicle (c), wall N: stucco floor and white lunette of the first style decoration, which dates back to the construction phase of the house in the second century BC. The holes in the beams that supported the vault are visible. The wall below was redecorated in the fourth style, with a white background with "small pictures representing birds, vases with supporting branches, etc." (Mau 1874).

5. Peristyle (h) summer coniltriclinium, with niches carved into the counter, circular tuff table and opus listatum columns covered with plaster. Wall W of the room (1), painted in red squares.  DAIR 312853

8. Triclinium (i), N wall decorated in the III style: black plinth "crosses", green horizontal stripe: middle area with two red side panels separated by a narrow black compartment with a red oval, central aedicule (on the right) with landscape. Warsher 60
7. Kitchen (k): oven built on the counter.
6. Summer triclinium (h): circular tuff table, perforated in the center for water jet. Warsher 55

10. 'Triclinium (i), S wall: central painting depicting an idyllic sacral landscape with a small temple, a statue of a female deity with modium on her head (Artemis?), an ithyphallic statue of Priapus, an offerer, shepherds and two goats (So, no. 684): state of conservation from the '30s.
9. Triclinium (i), wall E decorated in the III style: black plinth "crossed"; the central picture with Cassandra's Vaticinio in the middle area is missing. Warsher 61
11. Triclinium (i), S wall, central painting with idyllic sacral landscape: state of conservation of 1977.
12. Painting depicting the Vaticinium of Cassandra (So, no. 560), from the triclinium (1), wall E (see p. 59). Warsher 62; (National Museum of Naples, inv. 111476).

1. Tablinum (g): in the N-E corner there are very few traces of the fresco with a black plinth divided into squares and folders by carpet edges, and a white middle area with large panels bordered by large red bands. 77 N34412

2. Tablinum (g): as in the previous photo, here too we can see the small extension of the frescoed surface still preserved on the back wall of this room which was transformed with the closure of the large window originally

9. Triclinium (h): the S section of wall E is preserved almost entirely, even if very little can be read of the original decoration. The traces of the base of the metal candelabra that separates the central yellow panel from the red side panel can be distinguished, framed by a border of carpet in squares in the horizontal section and squares and rectangles in the vertical one. The oblique framing of the S wall clearly shows the effects of the washing action of atmospheric agents on the painted plaster. IV style.

7. Triclinium (h), wall E: the large gap in the plaster has led to the disappearance of the painting with edibles (see fig. 8) of which a minimal residue can be seen at the right end of the photo. The upper area (see figs. 11, 12) presented simple wooden architecture. IV style.

10. Triclinium (h): on the S wall, the entrance wall, there was a still life painting of Dionysian offerings. In fact, Discanno's drawing (1872) preserves the representation of an ox's head next to a plate of figs and dates (it is preferred to recognize this fruit rather than medlars, and because of its more elongated shape and because it is an exotic fruit alluding to a 'rich' offering), on which rests an olive branch, while an oinochòe and a pateretta rest lower between two intersecting thyrsis.
8. Triclinium (h), wall E: pencil reproduction by G. Discanno (pencil on paper 1872) of the painting with still life: molluscs and other unidentifiable edibles fall from an overturned basket.  ADS 6

11. Triclinium (h): the short and washed-out section of the upper area, preserved on wall E still allows a glimpse of the original decoration with wooden architectural elements, on a yellow background. IV style.
12. Triclinium (h); detail of the N-E angle. 77 N34420

13. The function of the room (u) as a triclinium, of square proportions and open towards the peristyle as if it were a wing, is confirmed by the recess for the bed on the E wall. The pictorial decoration is difficult to recognise, although the partitions of the wall with plinth, the middle area divided into red and yellow panels in the centre, and the upper area with architecture can still be distinguished. The reommento by A. Mau (BdI 1874, pp. 183-184) will make INS. 3, 3

14. Peristyle (x): portico E with brick columns covered with fluted red stucco, between which is the mouth of the cistern below. Probably the peristyle was also decorated in the third style, but nothing more remains of what little was still preserved in 1874.

1. Peristyle (e), western portico with brick columns connected to the corner pillars in opus vittatum by walls added at the back, and surmounted by arches in tuff ashlars that supported the vaulted roof of the portico. DAIR 312839

3. Cubicle (h), N wall, W section; the traces of the wooden aedicule of the red middle area are very clear, which continue in the upper area where it was connected to other thin architectural structures. 7. The oecus (r) instead underwent a redecoration around the middle of the first century AD, as evidenced by the presence of the stucco shell frame (?). IV style. 77 N34426

6. On a yellow plinth, the remains of a yellow panel to the S and a red one can be distinguished in the short W section of the wall with a door. II style.

8. In the small room (s), on the S wall where the recess for the bed is located, there are other traces of the II style decoration with the high yellow plinth divided into panels bordered in red, surmounted by a large red band. II style.

1. Cubicle (b): on the O wall there remains only a short stretch of the white middle area and the stucco frame with dentils, pertaining to a decoration of the first style.

2. Cubicle (e), wall N: much more is preserved in cubicle (e), in which a high red plinth with an upper edge of faux marble has replaced the original decoration in the first style that is preserved on the rest of the wall (see figs. 3 and 5). IV style.

3. Cubicle (e), wall N: the splayed window on this same wall has been closed so as not to allow the suture lines on the external façade to be distinguished. Inside, it interrupts the original white middle area with painted ashlars and a purple floor of the first style, but the closure was carried out at the same time as the decoration, as indicated by the superimposition of the stucco on the tompagno itself.
5. Cubicle (e), also on the S wall there is the red plinth with a faux marble border of the fourth style, restoration of the original ashlar decoration of the first style.
4. Cubicle (e), N wall, in the W section the subdivision into rows of ashlars, now discolored, of the middle and upper areas, with the purple plane, is even clearer. I style.

1. Atrium(d): table with marble top on masonry supports covered with plaster. 77 N34488

3. Atrium (d), on the W wall can be distinguished, below the later pictorial decoration, the frame structure with blocks of Sarno limestone, arranged with care and regularity. Very few traces are of the decoration on a white background with long ashlars outlined in red that imitates a decoration of the first style in the IV.

2. Room (b), wall N: even in the red plinth divided into two panels by a narrow central compartment, the bipartite scheme of the wall can be clearly read. The middle area is white, in the central corner you can see the traces of a thin candelabra.
4. Corridor (f), a plinth with a yellow background with red bands was the simple decoration in the second style on the wall O of this room.

6. Room (m), NW corner: a few more elements have remained in the room (m) although almost completely gone. The red middle area is divided into panels separated by narrow white bands and squared by stretched garlands. III style.

7. Cubicle (1), N-E corner: the red plinth with plants, divided into panels and compartments, is followed by the yellow middle area with panels bordered by edges of scaled carpet, with a vignette (traces of a cupid remain) and separated from each other by architectural glimpses (see fig. 8). IV style.

8. Cubicle (1) N-W corner: better than in the previous photo you can distinguish the architectural foreshortening that separated the yellow panels of the middle area with carpet edges (triangles in the vertical section and scales in the horizontal one). In the compartment on the N wall you can see the base perhaps of a vegetable candelabra. IV style.

1. Oecus (h), N wall, section W of the door: it is the only element of this wall photographed after the 1977 theft; This is the female acroterial figurine with cornucopia, ending in shoots, rendered in red monochrome with blue wings. AFS D26958

2. Oecus(h),S-E corner: at the time of the theft, only this reproduction could be used to identify the parts removed, which, although taken from a corner and of no particular quality, nevertheless clearly distinguished the scenography with figures of divinities (Apollo enthroned on the E wall and Hesperos on the S wall) in the central aedicules framed by doors, and warriors or servants behind partitions,  open doors or windows; in the upper area acroterial figures, candelabra, and paintings. This is the only photographic documentation of the gilded bronze statue of a warrior armed with a shield with chlamys and helmet, the type of which refers to the Ares Borghese, which was located to the right of the central aedicule, and of the acroterial figures

6. Oecus (h) wall E, central section: Apollo enthroned. In the drawing by N. The Fox (1870) the only substantial divergence from reality is in the representation of the throne which instead becomes a stool covered with cushions. Otherwise it is absolutely faithful to the original, at least as far as can be judged by what remains.

7. Oecus(h), S wall: an overall view of the S wall can only be found in the watercolour reproduced by von Cube, tav. II, and in a not very good photo of the DAIR (fig. below). Since it is the longest wall, the scenography that occupies the middle and upper areas is divided into seven elements of which the royal hall is an exedra with a coffered ceiling. From the open door, a male figure advances on the steps, only partially dressed in a cloak gathered on his left arm.
8. Oecus (h), S wall photographed in not good condition, however remains the only photographic evidence of the wall before the theft of 1977
9. The same wall after 1977.

The frieze continues on this wing with an episode taken from one of the cyclical poems, the Aethiopis of Arctinus, which narrates the arrival of the Amazons, led by Queen Penthesilea (IIevdeoAna), to help Priam (Ilpiapoc) and the Trojans. The inscriptions Ilevdeona and AyxUAeuc, found in fragments near this wall, must have referred to the same poem and in particular to the killing of the queen of the Amazons by Achilles. The arrival of Penthesilea in Troy is also represented in the same iconography on a fragment of the Tabula Iliaca and on fragments of sarcophagi lids, while it is presented with some variants on a group of terracotta cups of the Hellenistic age decorated in relief. An ovoli frame and, at the top, a frame surmounted by metal antefixes enclose the figuration. II style, phase II a.
